words.intro: In a German boardroom nothing is simply done. It’s brought to a conclusion, taken into consideration, placed at disposal. The longer the phrase, the further the chance that anyone will be blamed for it.

grammar[0].fact: A *Funktionsverbgefüge* can do things a plain verb can’t: *zur Anwendung kommen* is passive, *zur Anwendung bringen* is active, and *in Bewegung setzen* marks the moment something starts. That’s the defence. The attack is that it takes eleven syllables to say *use*.

grammar[1].fact: *Das gehört verboten!* is one of the most satisfying German sentences: *gehören* with a past form means it ought to be done, and usually that you’d like to see it done to somebody else. You’ll hear it on buses.

document.intro: A real model letter from a handbook for business people, about 1900, in Fraktur: a firm in Jena offers spirit levels to a firm in Spandau. Noun style at full steam: compare *unsere vorzügliche, maschinelle Einrichtung setzt uns in die Lage*.
document.fact: In the letters of the time you were *hochachtungsvoll*, full of high esteem, and today you are only *mit freundlichen Grüßen*. Your orders were *geschätzte Aufträge*. And firms still say *wir sind gern für Sie da*, which is a straight descendant of *stets gern zu Ihren Diensten*.
reading.intro: A meeting of the board. The subject is a coffee machine on the third floor, which has been broken for six months. Herr Dr. Blum opens the discussion. Max has been asked to take the minutes, and he has decided that from today, he’ll write down what’s actually said.
reading.fact: Germany has legally backed *Mitbestimmung*: in large companies, staff and union representatives sit on the supervisory board, up to half of the seats. So nearly any big decision goes through long meetings, and it can’t be pushed through as fast. On the other hand, it rarely gets pushed through wrong.
